title: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window
summary: Hidden Window describes adversaries suppressing the visible interface of a program so that nothing appears on screen while it runs. On Windows this is usually done with interpreter flags such as the hidden window style in PowerShell, or by writing Registry values that place console windows off screen. On macOS, property list keys can stop an application icon from appearing in the Dock. The behaviour leaves process creation telemetry showing an interpreter start with a hidden or non-interactive window flag, yet no corresponding user interface appears, which is what separates it from a user launching the same tool by hand.

beginner.definition: A hidden window is a program window that runs but cannot be seen. The application still works, but its window, its icon, or its console does not show on the screen. Attackers use this to run their tools without alarming the person using the computer.
beginner.whyItMatters: If you cannot see a program, you cannot notice that something is wrong. Malicious tools often run for hours in the background, and a visible window would give them away. Hidden windows also let an attacker keep working after the real user looks at the screen. Watching for quiet, invisible processes is therefore an important part of detection.
howItWorks: The attacker starts a program with an option that tells the system not to draw its window.
Windows scripting languages such as PowerShell, JScript and Visual Basic all offer this kind of option.
On macOS, a settings file called a property list can stop an application icon from showing in the Dock.
The Windows Registry can also be edited so console windows open outside the visible screen area.
Windows can create a second, hidden desktop where programs run with no visible desktop at all.
Detection depends on process logs showing the hidden option while the user reports seeing no window.
beginner.example: Imagine a shared office with a glass wall. You can normally see everyone through the glass. One day a colleague puts up a curtain and keeps working behind it. Work still happens behind it, and the chair still moves. But you can no longer see who is there or what they are doing. A hidden window is that curtain. The program keeps running and using the machine, so the computer still shows activity. Only the picture on the screen is missing, which is exactly what the attacker wants.
takeaways: A program with no visible window can still be running and causing harm.
Process logs often record hidden window options, so compare them with what the user saw.
Never assume that an empty screen means an idle computer.

objectives: Explain what a hidden window is and why an attacker would use one.
Describe how interpreter options such as a hidden window style suppress a program window.
Identify the log sources that record process creation and window style options.
Compare legitimate background administration with malicious hidden execution.
Suggest a detection idea that pairs process telemetry with reports from the user.
